I1.why: Reading the wave description as the moored buoy's own travel (direction plus phase speed as heading and speed) is a physical-model error that no shelf line names or closely resembles.

I2.why: Taking a sample statistic (significant height, peak period) as one individual wave is a close relative of the ecological fallacy, which reads an aggregate as an individual.

I3.why: It takes the 99/999/9999 fill values at face value as measurements, exactly the sentinel-as-real reading on the shelf.

I4.why: Treating waves as a current that carries the buoy at crest speed is a physics misreading that no shelf line names or comes close to.

I5.why: Reading a vertical statistical wave height as a horizontal distance travelled keeps the numbers but changes what they measure, a relative of the unit and axis swaps on the shelf.

I6.why: It reads the wind and pressure missing-value codes (99.0, 999, 9999.0) as real measurements of an eleven-month storm.

N01.quote: Where the buoy recorded nothing, as in the late-February to early-March outage, the line stops.

N03.quote: I read the file's fill values as data. NDBC writes 99, 999 or 9999 (with its decimals) in a column when there is no measurement.

N04.quote: Where the file holds its 99.00 placeholders the sea is simply left out

N06.quote: the wind and pressure columns turn to 99.0 and 9999.0 and never return ... the lines the file never wrote left black

N08.quote: After that the file holds only the placeholder nines for wind and pressure

N10.quote: The gap in February is where the buoy stopped reporting.

N11.quote: I read the file's missing-value codes as measurements.

N12.quote: The file holds no wind or pressure after that.
